content: Neuromuscular diseases (NMDs) are a diverse group of conditions that affect the anterior horn cells of the spinal cord, the neuromuscular junction, peripheral nerves, and muscles. These diseases often lead to physical disability, primarily due to progressive weakness in the limb muscles. In some cases, respiratory muscle weakness also occurs. Respiratory muscle training (RMT) has been proposed as a potential intervention to address respiratory muscle weakness, but its effects remain uncertain. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of RMT in individuals with NMD to guide clinical practice. The objective of this review was to assess the impact of RMT on individuals with NMD, including both adults and children, in comparison to sham training, no training, standard treatment, breathing exercises, or other variations of RMT. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs involving participants with NMD of any severity who were living in the community and not dependent on mechanical ventilation. The interventions studied included inspiratory muscle training (IMT), expiratory muscle training (EMT), or a combination of both. The review included 11 studies with a total of 250 participants diagnosed with various NMDs. These included three trials involving individuals with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), six trials involving individuals with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), one trial involving individuals with Becker muscular dystrophy (BMD) or limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, and one trial involving individuals with myasthenia gravis. Many of the trials had a high risk of bias, and there was significant variability in the populations, interventions, control groups, and outcome measures, which precluded meta-analysis in most cases. All included studies assessed lung capacity, which was the primary outcome of interest. However, four studies did not provide data for analysis, and none of the studies provided long-term data (over one year). Only one trial, conducted in individuals with ALS, reported information on adverse events. Outcomes such as unscheduled hospitalizations for chest infections or acute exacerbations of chronic respiratory failure were not reported. Measures of physical function and quality of life were reported in only one trial involving individuals with ALS. Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) Three trials compared RMT to sham training in individuals with ALS. Over a short-term period of 8 weeks, RMT did not result in a clear difference in the change in percent predicted forced vital capacity (FVC%) between the EMT and sham EMT groups (mean difference [MD] 0.70, 95% confidence interval [CI] -8.48 to 9.88; 46 participants; low-certainty evidence). After four months of treatment, IMT showed a mean difference in FVC% of 10.86% in favor of IMT (95% CI -4.25 to 25.97; 1 trial, 24 participants; low-certainty evidence), which exceeded the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) as estimated in individuals with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. However, there was no clear difference between IMT and sham IMT groups in physical functioning, as measured by the Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Functional Rating Scale (ALFRS) (MD 0.85, 95% CI -2.16 to 3.85; 1 trial, 24 participants; low-certainty evidence), or in quality of life, as measured by the EuroQol-5D (MD 0.77, 95% CI -17.09 to 18.62; 1 trial, 24 participants; low-certainty evidence) over the medium term (4 months). One trial reported that the IMT protocol did not result in adverse effects (very low-certainty evidence). Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) Two trials compared RMT to sham training in young males with DMD. In one study, the mean post-intervention total lung capacity (TLC) after 6 weeks favored RMT (MD 0.45 L, 95% CI -0.24 to 1.14; 1 trial, 16 participants; low-certainty evidence). In another trial, there was no clear difference in post-intervention FVC after 18 days between the RMT and sham RMT groups (MD 0.16 L, 95% CI -0.31 to 0.63; 1 trial, 20 participants; low-certainty evidence). One RCT and three cross-over trials compared RMT to no training in males with DMD, but the cross-over trials did not provide suitable data for analysis. Post-intervention (6-month) values showed no clear difference in percent predicted vital capacity (VC%) between the RMT and no training groups (MD 3.50, 95% CI -14.35 to 21.35; 1 trial, 30 participants; low-certainty evidence). Becker or Limb-Girdle Muscular Dystrophy One RCT involving 21 participants compared 12 weeks of IMT to breathing exercises in individuals with Becker or limb-girdle muscular dystrophy. The evidence was of very low certainty, and no definitive conclusions could be drawn. Myasthenia Gravis In individuals with myasthenia gravis, one trial compared RMT to breathing exercises. There was no clear difference in lung capacity, as measured by TLC, in the short term (MD -0.20 L, 95% CI -1.07 to 0.67; 1 trial, 27 participants; low-certainty evidence). The effects of RMT on quality of life were uncertain (1 trial, 27 participants). Some trials reported on the effects of RMT on inspiratory and/or expiratory muscle strength, but this evidence was also of low or very low certainty. Authors' Conclusions RMT may improve lung capacity and respiratory muscle strength in some NMDs. However, in ALS, RMT does not appear to have a clinically meaningful effect on physical functioning or quality of life, and it is unclear whether it causes adverse effects. Due to the clinical heterogeneity of the trials, the small number of participants, and the risk of bias, these findings should be interpreted with caution.
